Circular Poggendorf

GeometryCirclesParadoxes
Game: A circle is crossed by a strip with two straight edges; the pieces look as if they no longer fit together. There is nothing to win.
How to play: Drag the dot on the circle to change its size, or the dots on the strip's edges to move and widen it. Focus a dot and use the arrow keys, or press the buttons to show the whole circle.

Drag the three dots, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

Press "Show hidden circle": the pieces join into one round shape after all. The picture never changed — only what you can see of it did.

The claim, word for word

Bogomolny's page says: The parallel lines that obscure parts of a circle break the circle off so that its pieces do not appear to fit together. That is the claim kept here. Its first half is about geometry and can be checked. The words do not appear are about perception: no coordinate can measure how a picture looks, so the logic test does not pretend to. This is a circular form of the Poggendorff illusion; the page cites Shepard, Seckel and The Mind's Eye.

What the applet actually draws

One circle, centred on the canvas: drawOval(W/2 − R, H/2 − R, 2R, 2R). Then a strip painted in the background colour, fillRect(X0, 0, Width, H − 1), which erases the part of the circle behind it. Finally drawRect draws the same strip's outline, giving the two parallel vertical edges at x = X0 and x = X0 + Width. The circle's radius never changes and its centre stays at (W/2, H/2).

At an edge x, the circle meets it at y = H/2 ± √(R² − (x − W/2)²) — two ends, one if the edge just touches, none if it misses.

The two cut ends are symmetric about the horizontal middle line. Slide the strip away and the circle is whole: the pieces fit exactly. The test checks this over 8,000 configurations and compares every oval and strip with a second, literal transcription of the applet's own Draw() bytecode, plus 6,000 random settings of its three scrollbars.

Why the eye disagrees

The strip's edges are straight and run the whole height of the picture, so the eye treats them as the ends of the arcs and reads the two pieces as if they belonged to different circles. They do not: every point of the drawing is still exactly R from the centre. That gap between what is measured and what is seen is the optical illusion.

Deviation from the applet: the original had three scrollbars (radius, bar width and X0). Here three draggable dots do the same job. Their handles stay inside the drawing, so the largest circle reachable by dragging is 145 units (the scrollbar reached 500, where the circle overflowed), and the strip cannot be dragged past the right edge. All of the applet's ranges are still checked in the logic test, and the settings printed on its page (radius 125, width 50, X0 100) are the starting picture.

Widen the strip until it covers the circle completely: the pieces vanish and there is nothing left to misjudge. Then make it narrow again and press "Show hidden circle".
